what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including some skin cancers (melanoma), lung cancers, head and neck cancers, bladder cancers, and other cancers that your doctor has determined may respond to this treatment. It works by helping your immune system recognize and fight cancer cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the stomach area (abdomen). A healthcare provider will give you this injection at a clinic or infusion center. It is NOT given into a vein like the original IV form. Each injection takes only a few minutes. You do not give this medicine to yourself at home unless specifically trained and instructed by your healthcare team.
dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg given once every 6 weeks, injected under the skin. Your doctor may adjust the dose or schedule based on how you respond to treatment or if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose or schedule on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip an appointment, call your doctor or healthcare team as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to reschedule your missed dose as soon as you can. Do not try to double up or give yourself an extra dose to make up for the missed one. Your doctor will help get you back on schedule safely.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by the healthcare facility. If you are given any supplies to take home, keep them refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep it in the original packaging and away from light. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use if the medicine looks cloudy, discolored, or contains unusual particles.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as shingles vaccine, nasal flu spray, or yellow fever vaccine) while on this treatment without first talking to your doctor. Avoid taking corticosteroids or other immune-suppressing medicines without your doctor's knowledge, as they may reduce how well this medicine works. Tell your doctor before starting any new prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Let your doctor know if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: severe rash, blistering, or peeling skin; trouble breathing or shortness of breath; chest pain or irregular heartbeat; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea with blood; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or unusual tiredness; confusion, memory problems, or extreme weakness; vision changes; severe muscle pain or weakness; signs of infection such as fever or chills; severe swelling or pain at the injection site; or any other sudden or unusual symptoms. These may be signs of serious immune-related side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Cancer treatment with this medicine takes time. Some patients may begin to see benefits within a few weeks to a few months, while others may take longer. It is important to continue your treatment as scheduled even if you do not feel immediate changes. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups, blood tests, and imaging scans to see how well the treatment is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause harm to an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Older adults (65 years and older): No special dose adjustment is generally needed, but older adults should be closely monitored for side effects. Children and teenagers: Safety and effectiveness in patients under 18 years old have not been fully established for the subcutaneous form; ask your doctor. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will monitor you closely and may adjust your treatment if needed.
